prompt: Of the three titles this lesson compares, which names a level rather than a role?
hint: One of them measures trust, the other two describe a scope.

choices.text: Tech lead
choices.why: A tech lead is a role with its own scope: one team's delivery and technical direction.

choices.text: Senior engineer
choices.why: Right: senior says how far the company trusts somebody's judgement, and a senior engineer may hold either role or neither.

choices.text: Architect
choices.why: Architect is a role: the decisions that cross teams and hold for years. It is not the top rung of a ladder.

choices.text: Tech lead and architect together
choices.why: Those are the two roles of the lesson; the level is the third title.

prompt: Which two axes does the lesson use to tell the three roles apart?
hint: How much a decision touches, and for how long.

choices.text: Years of experience and salary band
choices.why: Those describe the person. The lesson places the decisions, and a person with many years may still work in one team's scope.

choices.text: Lines of code written and pull requests reviewed
choices.why: All three roles write and review code; activity counts do not separate them.

choices.text: Scope and horizon
choices.why: Right: how much of the system a decision touches, and how long it has to hold.

choices.text: Technical depth and people management
choices.why: People management is outside the architect's role altogether, as the last section says.

prompt: Match each of Will Larson's staff archetypes to the job it describes.
hint: One guides a team, one answers for an area, one goes from problem to problem, one extends an executive.

pairs.right: guides the approach and execution of one team
answers for the direction and quality of a critical area over time
goes deep into one hard problem after another
extends an executive's reach with borrowed authority

right_distractors: writes the performance reviews of the engineers in an area

prompt: Paula moves a slow test from the main suite to the nightly one, without asking anybody. By the lesson, is that right?
hint: Where does the decision sit on the two axes, and what does it cost to change?

choices.text: No: a change to the test suites affects quality, so the architect has to approve it
choices.why: Routing a cheap, local decision through the architect is the queue the lesson warns about.

choices.text: Yes: it sits inside her team and is cheap to undo
choices.why: Right: one team's scope, a short horizon, and a low cost of change. Being trusted with that is what senior means.

choices.text: No: her tech lead decides about tests, so she ought to have asked first
choices.why: A tech lead sets the team's direction; a senior engineer is trusted with decisions of this size inside it.

choices.text: Yes, because Platform owns the CI and so it owns every test in the company
choices.why: Owning the CI machinery does not make Platform the owner of other teams' tests. It is right for a different reason.

prompt: At another company, a staff engineer spends two quarters moving from one critical performance incident to the next, in whichever team has it, and leaves each once it is fixed. Which of Larson's archetypes is this?
hint: What does the person keep after the problem is gone?

choices.text: Architect: the incidents cross teams, so the work is architectural
choices.why: Crossing teams is part of it, but the architect has an area to answer for over time; this person leaves when each problem is solved.

choices.text: Right hand
choices.why: A right hand extends an executive's reach with borrowed authority; nothing here says they act for an executive.

choices.text: Solver
choices.why: Right: deep work on one hard problem after another, wherever the company needs it.

choices.text: Tech lead of each team in turn, since they guide the team while there
choices.why: A tech lead guides one team's approach and execution over quarters, not one incident at a time.

prompt: Order these Carreto decisions from the shortest horizon to the longest.
hint: How long does each one have to hold before somebody revisits it?
items: Which failing test Ícaro fixes first today
How the Pix payout work is cut into tickets this sprint
Which retry library Payments standardises on this quarter
Which team owns the drivers' payout data for the coming years
trap: The data ownership question looks like a technical detail, but it crosses teams and holds for years, which is why it is the architect's.

prompt: Why did it work, in Carreto's second year, for Tomás to hold all three roles?
hint: Think about where a decision falls when roles are split.

choices.text: With one head holding all the context, no decision fell between roles
choices.why: Right: there was no gap between roles, because there was one person in every conversation.

choices.text: Six engineers took no architectural decisions
choices.why: They took plenty, including how the monolith was divided. The decisions were there; the gaps were not.

choices.text: He had the CTO title, so his decisions carried formal authority
choices.why: The title did not make the arrangement work; at eighteen engineers he still had it and the arrangement failed.

choices.text: A monolith needs no architecture until it is split into services
choices.why: A monolith has an architecture too, as lesson 1 and lesson 2 both argue; dividing it into modules was one of his decisions.

prompt: Kátia and Renata spent two weeks arguing about Matching reading Pricing's tables. By the lesson, what took the time?
hint: Each was right on her own axis.

choices.text: Working out whether 40 ms was really faster than 400 ms
choices.why: Nobody disputed the measurement; the speed-up was real.

choices.text: Not knowing whose question it was
choices.why: Right: each conversation reopened who decides before it reached the substance, which is what a decision-rights table removes.

choices.text: Pricing's team refusing to say how its tables were laid out
choices.why: Nothing in the case says Pricing refused anything; the dispute was between Matching and the architect.

choices.text: Kátia lacking the seniority to propose a cross-team change
choices.why: Under the advice process anybody may propose and even take a decision after asking; seniority was not the obstacle.

prompt: In Carreto's decision-rights table, who decides a new event that Tracking publishes and Payments consumes?
hint: It is a contract between two teams' services.

choices.text: The architect alone, because it crosses a team boundary
choices.why: Crossing a boundary makes the architect someone to ask; for a contract the table gives the decision to the two tech leads.

choices.text: Tracking's team, since the publisher owns the event
choices.why: A contract binds both sides; the consumer has as much at stake as the publisher.

choices.text: The two tech leads together, after asking the architect
choices.why: Right: that is the third row. The architect is asked first and the consuming teams are told.

choices.text: Helena, because the event changes what drivers see
choices.why: Product decides what gets built next, not the shape of the contract between two services.

prompt: The decision-rights table does not replace the advice process: anybody may still take a decision after asking, and the table says who ___ for it.
hint: The verb for accountability.

prompt: Platform wants to replace the message broker three teams use with a managed queue from the cloud provider. Under Carreto's table, how is this decided?
hint: Which row covers a new piece of infrastructure in production?

choices.text: Platform decides, since it operates the broker and will operate the queue
choices.why: Operating it is why Platform must be asked; the teams that run on it are affected too, and the row gives the decision to the architect.

choices.text: The architect decides, after asking Platform and the three teams
choices.why: Right: a new broker in production is the fifth row, and everybody is told in the forum.

choices.text: The three tech leads vote, and Platform implements what wins
choices.why: The table has no vote in it; it names who answers for each kind of decision.

choices.text: Tomás decides it, as any change of supplier needs the CTO
choices.why: Tomás is told about data ownership in the table, and nothing gives him this row.

prompt: Which of these are warning signs that one person holding all three roles has stopped working? Choose all that apply.
hint: The lesson lists three, seen at eighteen engineers.

choices.text: Changes wait days for that one person's review
choices.why: Yes: decisions queueing behind one calendar.

choices.text: Two teams find out about each other's choices in production
choices.why: Yes: the tax-number field added twice with different validation.

choices.text: Design reviews start raising more questions than before
choices.why: More questions in a review is a healthy sign, and the lesson does not list it.

choices.text: That person's own code is the code most often reverted
choices.why: Yes: written between meetings, it shows the person doing none of the roles well.

choices.text: The company hires a second product manager
choices.why: That is growth on the product side and says nothing about how the engineering roles are held.

prompt: Which of these lies outside the architect's role, by the lesson?
hint: Four boundaries, and one of them is about people.

choices.text: Deciding who owns which data across teams
choices.why: That is one of the two rows the table gives the architect.

choices.text: Keeping the technical risk register
choices.why: The risk register from lesson 14 is listed among what stays inside the boundary.

choices.text: Reading a sample of pull requests each week
choices.why: Reading a sample keeps the architect calibrated (lesson 15); approving each one is what lies outside.

choices.text: Writing the engineers' performance reviews
choices.why: Right: that belongs to the engineering managers, and holding it makes disagreeing with the architect expensive.

prompt: A company merges 180 pull requests a week, and its architect would spend 12 minutes on each. How many hours a week would approving them take?
hint: Pull requests times minutes, then divide by 60.

prompt: Helena wants drivers paid by Pix the moment the proof of delivery arrives. What is Renata's part?
hint: Who owns what Carreto builds next?

choices.text: Turn it down, because instant payment adds risk to Payments
choices.why: Risk is something to state and price; refusing turns a product decision into the architect's.

choices.text: Approve it, since drivers asked for it and the product director agrees
choices.why: Approving is not hers to do either; the decision is Helena's, informed by the cost.

choices.text: Delay the estimate until the 24-hour flow has been rewritten
choices.why: Holding back an estimate is taking the product decision by other means.

choices.text: Show the structural cost, then let Helena decide
choices.why: Right: making the structural cost visible is the architect's job; choosing is product's.

prompt: Why does the lesson keep people management away from the architect, even where a manager would make a fine architect?
hint: What happens to the developer who wants to say "that will not work"?

choices.text: Managers lack the time to keep up with the code their teams write
choices.why: The lesson's argument is about disagreement, not about time.

choices.text: Disagreement gets costly, so advice becomes instruction
choices.why: Right: the architect loses the developer who would have caught the bad decision early.

choices.text: Labour law forbids one person from both rating and directing engineers
choices.why: No law is involved; it is about what the combination does to disagreement.

choices.text: Engineering managers outrank architects in Carreto's chart
choices.why: Rank is not the argument; the table gives each its rows without ranking them.

prompt: In the sprint where Renata held the Pix adapter ticket, the release was planned for day 8 and happened on day 13. How many working days late was it?
hint: Subtract the planned day from the actual one.

prompt: Renata wants to write code in Payments next sprint to stay calibrated. Which choice keeps her off the critical path?
hint: Which task does no release wait on?

choices.text: Pair with Ícaro on the refund endpoint while he keeps the ticket
choices.why: Right: she gets the feel of the code, and the task stays with someone whose week is predictable.

choices.text: Take the refund endpoint ticket, which the release depends on
choices.why: That is the Pix adapter sprint again: the release would wait on the week most likely to be taken by something else.

choices.text: Review and approve each of the team's pull requests that sprint
choices.why: That moves her from the critical path of one ticket to the critical path of all of them.

choices.text: Split the endpoint and keep the half the tests start from
choices.why: Holding the half that others start from is still being what the release waits for.

prompt: Match each Carreto decision to who decides it under the decision-rights table.
hint: Two of the seven rows belong to the architect.

pairs.left: the logging library inside the Driver app's backend
pairs.right: the team, through its tech lead

pairs.left: whether Shipper may read Payments' invoice tables
whether the instant-payment feature is built this quarter
moving Ícaro from Payments to Tracking

right_distractors: a vote of all seven tech leads

prompt: Which decisions does the lesson say are the architect's to answer for?
hint: The test from lesson 6, applied to a person.

choices.text: The most technically difficult ones in any team
choices.why: Difficulty is not the test: a hard problem inside one team belongs to that team, or to a solver.

choices.text: Those that cross a team boundary or cost a lot to change
choices.why: Right: scope and horizon, which is why most of the table belongs to the teams.

choices.text: Any decision about which technology a team uses
choices.why: A library inside one service is the team's; only a new language, database or broker in production is the architect's row.

choices.text: Those the CTO delegates to her each quarter
choices.why: The role is defined by the kind of decision, not by a list handed down each quarter.

prompt: A company of nine engineers has one tech lead and no architect. She is deciding whether the billing and the scheduling modules will share a database. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: Name the hat.

choices.text: Hire an architect before taking a decision of that size
choices.why: The lesson says the title can wait; a company of nine needs the habits, not a new hire.

choices.text: Decide it with the next sprint's tickets, as the team is small
choices.why: That is taking an architectural decision in the same breath as which ticket goes first, which is what the lesson warns against.

choices.text: Leave it to the developers of the two modules to agree between themselves
choices.why: Two modules sharing data is a cross-cutting decision; leaving it to whoever moves first is how decisions fall between chairs.

choices.text: Treat it as architectural: ask those affected, write it down, put a number on it
choices.why: Right: the tech lead says which hat she is wearing and gives the decision the course's treatment.

prompt: Diego, the Driver app's tech lead, wants the app to call Tracking's API directly for positions instead of going through the Driver backend. Who decides, by Carreto's table?
hint: Is this inside one team, or a contract between two?

choices.text: Diego, because the change is inside the Driver app's own code
choices.why: The code change is Driver's, but the app would become a client of Tracking's API, which is a contract between two teams.

choices.text: Renata alone, as the architect
choices.why: She must be asked first; the table gives contracts to the two tech leads.

choices.text: Diego and Tracking's tech lead together, after asking Renata
choices.why: Right: a new consumer of an API is a contract between two teams' services, the third row.

choices.text: Platform, because the app's network traffic will change
choices.why: Network traffic may concern Platform, but no row makes it the decider of a contract between Driver and Tracking.
